THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Buddhist temples, monasteries and networks

Buddhism arose in South Asia in the first millennium BCE. Over many centuries, worshippers, translators and rulers created distinct religious landscapes across Asia. A stupa at Sanchi, a manuscript from Dunhuang and the Great Buddha at Nara show different ways people built communities around Buddhist practice.

Selected institutions from South Asia to Sri Lanka, Tibet, eastern Asia and Southeast Asia. Site ages identify particular monuments or phases of use. They often postdate the earliest local Buddhist communities.

The Buddha and the places of pilgrimage

Buddhist traditions connect Siddhartha Gautama’s awakening to Bodh Gaya and his birth to Lumbini. His exact lifetime is debated, but Buddhism’s origins lie several centuries before the Common Era. The Aśokan pillar at Lumbini records a royal visit in the third century BCE, placing a pilgrimage tradition in the historical record centuries after the Buddha’s life. [3] [4] [1]

Teachings about suffering, ethical conduct and paths to liberation traveled through oral instruction, texts and communities of practice. Stupas could hold relics or commemorate a person or event. Walking clockwise around a stupa made worship a physical practice. Sanchi’s original Mauryan monument was enlarged, and its gates and sculpture belong to later periods of investment. [1] [6] [2]

Who supported a monastery?

Buddhist communities depended on relations between people who left household life and people who provided food, property, money or labor. Commissioning an image or monument and giving to a community were ways of seeking religious merit. At Indian sites, inscriptions preserve gifts from laypeople and from monks and nuns. The named sponsors of images make the economic and devotional roles of women visible. [10] [1] [2]

In Sri Lanka, Anuradhapura combined royal patronage with longstanding monastic communities. The sacred Bodhi tree is revered as a descendant of the tree at Bodh Gaya. The tradition linking those trees made a South Asian place of awakening present in the ritual and political life of another island capital. [9] [4]

A ninth-century copperplate from Nalanda records King Devapāla’s grant of five villages at the request of Bālaputradeva, a ruler based in Sumatra. The grant supported the monks, the monastery’s upkeep and the copying of texts. It ties an Indian monastery to patrons across the Bay of Bengal and to the agricultural resources that sustained scholarship on the ground. [27] [28]

Learning, copying and translation

At Nalanda, monks lived and studied in a network of brick monasteries and shrines. The seventh-century Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied there. His travels and writing connect a specific institution with the movement of teachers, books and pilgrims across linguistic and political frontiers. [7] [8] [1] [29]

Dunhuang’s caves preserve painted ritual settings and manuscripts from successive regimes at a Silk Roads oasis. A printed Diamond Sutra dated 868 names Wang Jie in its colophon and records that he had it made for distribution on behalf of his parents. This surviving book shows how copying and circulating a scripture could express family devotion and make religious merit visible. [11] [12] [13]

Courts, communities and political risk

Longmen’s patrons cut individual niches and enormous sculptures into cliffs near Luoyang. At Nara, Emperor Shōmu’s government supported Tōdai-ji and provincial temples and nunneries. Such projects brought together resources, ritual specialists and artisans to make Buddhism visible within political life. [14] [17] [16]

Patronage could be withdrawn. Tang emperor Wuzong’s edict of 845 ordered the suppression of Buddhist institutions. Its language shows rulers treating the wealth, buildings and personnel of monasteries as political and economic issues. The edict records one government’s position in a particular crisis. [15] [1]

Maritime worlds and changing landscapes

Buddhist teachers, texts and images also traveled through Indian Ocean and Southeast Asian ports. Theravāda lineages became influential in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia, while institutions shaped by Mahāyāna and esoteric teachings developed in other places. Their histories intersected with Hindu courts and local traditions. These broad designations cover many different communities and ritual practices. [23] [2] [25]

Borobudur’s terraces guide visitors past reliefs and stupas. Bagan’s monuments fill a capital’s surrounding landscape. At Angkor Wat, a temple built for Vishnu later housed Buddhist worship. In Tibet, institutions such as the Potala linked particular Buddhist lineages to government. These sites show how communities made different uses of architecture and political sponsorship over time. [18] [19] [21] [22] [24] [26]

Places and periods

The date of a monument, dedication or rebuilding provides a specific anchor for each place. Early traditions and later layers of use can belong to the same site. [4] [6] [21]

Originals and translations · ordinary lives in writing

Payments, animals, deliveries, disputes, household instructions and the occasional celebration. Originals appear as artifact photographs or credited original-language transcriptions; a transcription uses modern type, not an imitation of an ancient hand. Each English excerpt is labeled and linked to its edition.

Medieval Chinese · Association circular

Late for the feast, owe a beaker of wine

886 CE, Late Tang · Mogao Cave 17, near Dunhuang, Gansu, China
British Library Or.8210/S.1453, verso

A local association asks its members to assemble near Jiejia Hermitage for an annual meeting and feast. The circular was passed among members, and a person who skipped the event entirely owed a larger fine.

Original-language text

如右(有)於時不到者，罰酒壹角。

Chinese-character transcription from the verso of a copy of the Diamond Sutra. Parentheses preserve the editor’s reading of a character.

Imre Galambos, adapting Lionel Giles · Original source · Public domain ancient wording

English translation · excerpt

Those who do not arrive punctually will be fined one beaker (jiao) of wine
